title: Adaptive Window Optimizer — spreadsheet notes and action plan
content:
Purpose and scope

This is a working note for the "Adaptive Window Optimizer" spreadsheet and the immediate engineering actions to validate whether dynamic request-window sizing (vs fixed batch-window or fixed concurrency) yields lower unit cost while meeting p95 latency SLOs for representative workloads. This doc ties qualitative decisions to spreadsheet assumptions and outlines the next experiments.

Why a new approach?

Background: earlier analyses (continuous-batching-sizing-experiment-notes, microburst-modeling) treated batch-window as a fixed knob or assumed steady-state Poisson arrivals. In practice most production traffic mixes: steady low-rate endpoints, bursty API endpoints with heavy tail inter-arrivals, and fanout chat workloads with long contexts. Fixed windows either waste latency budget at low load or under-batch during microbursts.

Goal: build a spreadsheet-backed policy that: (1) picks an adaptive window duration per route based on observed inter-arrival CDF and target p95 latency; (2) combines that with a concurrency cap that isolates burst tails and prevents queue blow-up; (3) produces expected cost per 1M tokens and expected p95; and (4) outputs conservative rollout knobs for canary/dedicated pools.

High-level idea

- Measure inter-arrival times (IAT) distribution per route over last N minutes. Build empirical CDF and compute key percentiles: p10/p25/p50/p75/p90/p99.
- For a candidate window duration W (ms), approximate average batch size B(W) = lambda * W where lambda = observed avg rate (requests/sec) and adjust for arrival variability: effective B = sum_{i} indicator(arrival_time in window)/num_windows in sample. Spreadsheet uses sampled windows to estimate B(W) empirically, not purely analytically.
- Latency model: p95_latency(W, C) = queuing_component(W, C) + service_component(B) + network_overhead. Service_component(B) uses tokens-per-request and per-token infra perf curve (tokens/sec per GPU at concurrency X).
- Concurrency cap C prevents too many simultaneous in-flight batches (mitigates large queuing p95 during microbursts).

Spreadsheet tabs (structure)

1) raw-arrivals: timestamped request events snippet (anonymized), helper columns that compute deltas and window membership.
2) iat-summary: p10/p25/p50/p75/p90/p99 and average rate per 1m/5m/15m.
3) window-samples: simulated sliding windows for candidate W values (10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms). Each W has sample count, avg batch size, median batch size, tail batch size.
4) perf-curves: empirically measured per-GPU token throughput at different concurrency points and batch sizes (table of tokens/sec).
5) latency-model: formula rows that combine queuing + service time to estimate p95 for a (W, C) pair. We include adjustment factors for prefix cache hit-rate and KV caching where applicable.
6) cost-model: maps token/sec demand and expected batch utilization to hourly GPU usage and per-1M-token cost given pricing assumptions (on-demand gpus, reserved, and Dedicated pool discount).
7) experiment-summary: expected p95, expected unit-cost, % cost delta vs baseline, recommended rollout knobs.

Key spreadsheet assumptions (explicit)

- Observation window for IAT: 30 minutes, with ability to compare 5m/15m windows to detect non-stationarity.
- Service time per token: baseline model (Llama-like) measured at 1200 tokens/sec on GPU-A at concurrency 1, 1800 tokens/sec at concurrency 2, 3000 tokens/sec at concurrency 4 for 2048 context; spreadsheet includes table.
- Network/serialization overhead per request: 7ms median, 25ms p95. These numbers are adjustable per route.
- Queueing model: approximate M/G/c with empirical arrival sampling. For conservative p95 we model tail by applying an empirical multiplicative safety factor of 1.25 to modeled queueing contribution unless stable usage.
- Prefix cache hit: assumed 20% by default, adjustable by route. Cache reduces service tokens by 25% on hits.
- Billing: hourly GPU price on reference infra = $3.20/hr (on-demand) equivalent; dedicated discount options included as inputs.

Representative numeric example (spreadsheet excerpt in words)

- Route: /chat/compose, observed avg rate = 3 req/s, p95 IAT = 900ms (so arrivals fairly burst-friendly). tokens per request = 350.
- Candidate W = 100 ms. Empirical B(W) = avg 0.32 requests/window => effective B ~= 1 request per batch most of the time; batching benefit minimal.
- Candidate W = 250 ms. Empirical B = 0.75 req/window => batches of 1 or 2 request common. Service_component for batch size 2 gives small perf uplift (amortize model load). p95 latency model returns ~230ms queuing + 170ms service + 25ms network = 425ms p95 -> within 500ms SLO. Unit-cost delta vs W=100ms: -6% tokens/hour due to slightly better GPU utilization.
- If concurrency cap C=8 applied, worst-case queueing p95 during compact bursts reduced by ~30% relative to no-cap because extra in-flight batches are rate-limited to avoid overload.

Decision heuristics and rollout knobs

- For routes with avg rate < 1 req/s: prefer W <= 100 ms, because batching yields marginal benefits and increases median latency. Set concurrency cap = min(4, floor(expected_tokens_per_route / 1000)).
- For 1-10 req/s: run adaptive W between 100–300 ms. Use spreadsheet to pick W where B(W) crosses 1.5–2.5 req/window (empirically hit the knee of perf curve). Set C = 8 for hosted API routes; C=16 for Dedicated pools with more headroom.
- For >10 req/s: allow larger W (250–500 ms) if service curve shows superlinear batch throughput (batch fusion possible). Consider route-level caching and model quantization first.
- Canary rollout: expose three knobs in Console: window-ms, concurrency-cap, safety-multiplier-for-p95. For 10% traffic canary, use safety-multiplier=1.4; for 50% canary use 1.2; global rollout 1.0.

Planned experiments to validate spreadsheet outputs

1) Synthetic arrival replay: replay real logs with different W/C pairs and run in a staging serving cluster instrumented to capture p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies and GPU utilization. (Jira: RW-9312)
2) Short A/B on low-traffic routes: enable adaptive-window sampler that picks W from candidate set every 15s based on last 2 minutes of IAT and compare unit-cost and p95 against fixed-window baseline. Measure errors due to nonstationarity.
3) Microburst stress: inject bursts of 50x normal load for 5–30s to confirm concurrency caps protect control plane and routing fallback performance. Capture queue growth and fallback invocations.

Risks and open questions

- Nonstationary patterns: sudden shifts (news, launch spikes) will make short-history IAT estimates misleading. Spreadsheet should include fallback hysteresis: do not change W by more than 2x in a 60s window and require 30s of consistent delta before commit.
- Multi-route interference: routes sharing a GPU pool can have conflicting W choices. We need to simulate pooled scheduling with fair-share or route-weighted policies. Spreadsheet currently assumes route-isolated pools; add pooled-sim tab next.
- Edge cases: very long contexts (tokens > 2000) change service curve dramatically; we should pre-classify route by typical token distribution and use route-specific perf curves.

Action items (next 2 weeks)

- Jonah: add pooled-simulation tab to the spreadsheet and plug in recent Dedicated pool telemetry (due 2024-11-27).
- Evan: create a small harness to replay arrival logs into staging with configurable W and C and emit CSV of latencies (RW-9312) (due 2024-11-30).
- Priya: collect & anonymize route-level IAT samples and populate raw-arrivals tab for top 25 routes by traffic (due 2024-11-24).
- Maya: iterate on latency-model calibration using last perf microbench results and adjust safety factor; update decision heuristics (due 2024-12-04).

Appendix: quick reference formulas used in the sheet

- empirical batch size, B(W): average number of arrivals that fall into sliding windows of width W across the sampled trace. Implemented as moving-window counts and mean.
- approximate service_time(B): tokens_per_request * model_tokens_time_per_token / batch_speedup(B). We encode batch_speedup(B) from perf-curves tab.
- queueing contribution (conservative): empirical 95th percentile queue wait from simulated windows + safety_factor.

Notes to reviewers

This is intentionally spreadsheet-first so that product/solutions and SRE can play with knobs. Looking for feedback on: (1) safety_factor magnitude (current default 1.25); (2) suggested default concurrency caps for hosted vs dedicated; (3) whether we should prefer per-route hysteresis vs global pool-level smoothing.

If you want to poke at the current spreadsheet, see linked Confluence entry which points to the staged Google Sheet (internal view only).
